# First aid and resuscitation (`first_aid_resuscitation`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/medicine.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Medicine & hygiene (`medicine`)
- Deps: helped by blood_circulation, wound_care
- Core idea: Get help and check breathing. For an unresponsive adult who is not breathing normally or is only gasping, start chest compressions in the centre of the chest, 100–120 per minute, about 5–6 cm deep, letting the chest rise fully. Use a defibrillator as soon as available. A trained rescuer provides two breaths for every thirty compressions; rescue breaths are especially important after drowning. Place an unconscious person who is breathing normally on their side and keep checking breathing. Apply firm direct pressure to severe bleeding. Cool a burn with clean running water for twenty minutes and cover it.
- Pitfalls:
  - Period methods for the drowned: hanging by the feet, rolling over a barrel, blowing tobacco smoke into the bowel
  - Pouring drink into the mouth of an unconscious person
  - Butter, oil, flour or dung on burns
  - Forcing something between the teeth of someone in a fit
  - Promising that chest compression revives the dead; without a defibrillator most cardiac arrests stay fatal
- History: europe: 1732 – Tossach revives a suffocated miner by mouth-to-mouth breathing (published 1744); 1767 Amsterdam society for rescuing the drowned; 1774 Royal Humane Society, London; 1790s Larrey's flying ambulances and sorting of the wounded by urgency; 1863 Red Cross; 1877–1882 St John Ambulance and Esmarch's first-aid courses for laymen; americas: 1958 – Safar and Elam prove mouth-to-mouth beats the arm-lift methods; 1960 Kouwenhoven, Jude and Knickerbocker introduce closed-chest compression; 1974 Heimlich's abdominal thrust
- Read:
  - Peter Safar, Lourdes A. Escarraga and James O. Elam, A comparison of the mouth-to-mouth and mouth-to-airway methods of artificial respiration with the chest-pressure arm-lift methods, New England Journal of Medicine (1958)
  - W. B. Kouwenhoven, James R. Jude and G. Guy Knickerbocker, Closed-chest cardiac massage, Journal of the American Medical Association (1960)
  - Mickey S. Eisenberg, Life in the Balance: Emergency Medicine and the Quest to Reverse Sudden Death (1997)
